newsitem.title: USA: U.S. may resume ag export subsidies soon- official.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may resume ag export subsidies soon- official.

text.p: The United States may resume subsidized sales of some grain exports yet this year, ending a two-year hiatus, the Agriculture Department official in charge of export programs said Wednesday.

During a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing, the official, Gus Schumacher, said export subsidies would be used "if we need it" and said the Agriculture Department would scrutinize European Union grain tenders in coming weeks to see if it unfairly subsidized grain sales.

There also were signs the Clinton administration was nearing a decision whether to subsidize sales of wheat flour and malt barley. A proposal reportedly was under study at the sub-cabinet level, usually the decision-making point.
"We're hopeful that will be resolved shortly," Chris Goldthwait, the department's sales manager, told reporters but declined to forecast the outcome or when it would be made.
The EU has made some recent discount grain sales but at nominal rates that have not necessitated a U.S. response. Europe was on track for a large grain harvest this fall.
Schumacher told senators it "may very well be" that the department would resume use of the Export Enhancement Program before the end of the year.

He appealed for large funding for EEP, the major U.S. farm export subsidy. The White House requested $500 million for the fiscal year beginning October 1 but Congress appeared likely to provide less than half of that.
"We need to have that tool in reserve if the Europeans start to grab market share in markets we need, like Egypt," Schumacher said.
Three wheat-state senators faulted the department for not using EEP in the past year. After a couple of years of tight supplies, U.S. prices have started to fall, they said.

"If conditions warrant, as they very well may in the coming year, we will be very aggressive in using" export programs, Schumacher replied, later adding, "We will use it (EEP) if we need it and only if we need it."
The United States has not subsidized a grain sale in two years due to a run of high prices and an EU decision to curtail its subsidies.
